quote: But compulsion is not a property of arguments; it is a property of minds that process arguments.
content: This is true, universally conceded, and beside the point of the views it is aimed at. Moral rationalists such as Kant, Korsgaard (The Sources of Normativity, 1996) and Parfit (On What Matters, 2011; books, no DOI) do not claim that sound arguments causally compel every physical system. They claim that reasons apply to every rational agent, whether or not the agent is moved by them. The essay shows that some possible minds won't be persuaded. It doesn't show that those minds are making no mistake, which is the actual question. Throughout, "compelling" slides back and forth between its causal sense and its normative sense.

quote: For every lawful causal system that zigs at a set of points, you should be able to specify another causal system that lawfully zags at the same points.
content: This argument can't tell morality from mathematics. There is equally a physical system that, shown a proof that there are infinitely many primes, outputs "false." So there is no universally compelling argument for arithmetic either. The author doesn't conclude that arithmetic lacks objective truth, so the argument has no bearing on whether morality does. Philosophers call this a companions-in-guilt argument (Cuneo, The Normative Web, 2007; book, no DOI): any consideration that impugns moral objectivity merely because dissenting minds could exist impugns epistemic and mathematical objectivity just as much.

quote: Many philosophers are convinced that because you can in-principle construct a prior that updates to any given conclusion on a stream of evidence, therefore, Bayesian reasoning must be “arbitrary,”
content: The philosophers go unnamed, and the serious objection isn't the one answered. The technical worry about priors is not that they fail to persuade a ghost of perfect emptiness. It is that they can fail to converge. Diaconis & Freedman (1986) showed that in infinite-dimensional problems a Bayesian with a reasonable-looking prior can stay inconsistent forever, never learning the truth however much data arrives. Whether priors "wash out" depends on the particular priors and models, and there are theorems on both sides. Recasting the objection as a demand for argument from nothing lets the essay skip it.

quote: like the argument I use to make people let the AI out of the box
content: The footnote says "Just kidding," but the AI-box experiments recur across the sequences as evidence about superintelligent persuasion, and they aren't evidence. The transcripts were never released, the participants were self-selected enthusiasts, and by the author's own later account he lost some of the subsequent games. An experiment whose rules forbid publishing its data, and whose results are reported only by the experimenter, can't support a claim about "argument sequences that would compel any neurologically intact human."

quote: And then Wright converted to Christianity— yes, seriously. So you really don’t want to fall into this trap!
content: A novelist's later religious conversion is offered as a warning about where belief in universal moral arguments leads. That is guilt by biography: an argument from a single case, with no mechanism, and the sequence elsewhere names both as errors. Kant, Parfit, Korsgaard and Nagel all hold that moral truths bind every rational agent, and none of them was a Christian; Wright's conversion tells us about Wright. In the 2020 PhilPapers survey moral realism was the view of a clear majority of professional philosophers (Bourget & Chalmers 2023), and the essay answers that majority with one novelist's biography.
